claims.text: An intermediate grain size optimizes high-temperature plastic strain in gradient-nanograined CoCrNi medium-entropy alloys.
An intermediate grain size optimizes high-temperature toughness in gradient-nanograined CoCrNi medium-entropy alloys.
The proposed optimum arises because intermediate grain sizes promote controlled grain-boundary sliding.
Excessive grain-boundary density can cause localized overheating.
Insufficient grain-boundary density limits grain-boundary sliding.
Controlled thermomechanical treatments can generate CoCrNi samples spanning ultra-nanograined through coarse-grained states.
Quantifying dislocation density and secondary phases can help determine whether grain-boundary-network changes are isolated from these confounders.
Temperatures of approximately 700–800°C are relevant to the intended fusion plasma-facing-component application.
Grain-boundary character and density govern the activation and efficacy of grain-boundary sliding during high-temperature deformation.
Grain-boundary sliding is a dominant high-temperature plastic-deformation mechanism in nanostructured alloys.
Grain-boundary sliding relieves strain localization.
An optimal grain-boundary density balances beneficial sliding against boundary-localized overheating.
Ultra-small grains and their associated high boundary area may cause localized thermal instability.
Coarse grains provide insufficient grain-boundary sliding, thereby promoting strain localization and brittle failure.
Plastic strain will show a pronounced peak at an intermediate grain size relative to ultra-nanograined and coarse-grained samples.
Toughness will show a pronounced peak at an intermediate grain size relative to ultra-nanograined and coarse-grained samples.
The proposed effect is bounded to fully dense CoCrNi tested at approximately 700–800°C under conditions where grain-boundary sliding dominates.
Dislocation density, texture, and secondary-phase formation may confound the relationship between grain size and mechanical performance.
Failure to observe an intermediate-grain-size peak in both plastic strain and toughness would falsify the hypothesis.
Attribution of improved performance to dislocation-density or secondary-phase changes rather than grain-boundary-sliding activity would falsify the proposed mechanism.
